spacertales-sable-freight-file.name: SABLE_FREIGHT.TXT
spacertales-sable-freight-file.text:
SABLE MARGIN: FREIGHT NOTE COPY
Retained by Neri Vale

The clean copy lists service records, quantity six. The handwritten copy lists drain cans, quantity six. Neither copy names a model. The number of containers agrees. Their supposed job does not.

First claimant: the contents were part of office provision and remained contractor property.

Second claimant: the consignment replaced process equipment against a different finance schedule and remained its property.

Crew account: the old cans were ours. The new shipment was held against an unpaid account. We kept using the old ones, repaired what could be repaired, and bought two replacements out of wages. None of that appears on either finance schedule.

A later catalogue comparison establishes that a drain can holds process contents. It does not establish which cans arrived, which went aboard or who paid for any of them. The present-day example was retained by its owner.

I have crossed out service records on the description line and left both ownership claims untouched. That is a correction, not a judgement.

The crew's first covering letter was omitted from the clean file because it arrived after the account was closed. The account was closed before the crew were paid. I am attaching the letter anyway.

Note for [player-first]: if somebody asks whether this proves their version, please give them the whole answer. It proves why the description needed correcting. It also proves that three accounts were submitted, rather than the two the claimants preferred.

Neri

Pencil note below the signature: a useful mistake is still a mistake.

spacertales-yard-signatures-file.name: YARD_SIGNATURES.TXT
spacertales-yard-signatures-file.text:
REPAIR LETTERS: SABLE MARGIN
Copied by permission of the former shift crew

We were told the refit was replacement pending. The machinery had another shift to do before the replacement arrived. Then another. We worked the parts we had.

The company inventory records a recovery plant. Ours records a fixture bought used, a reclaimer put right after delivery, bins supplied with the wrong freight note and a furnace that took longer to earn back its price than anybody promised. The equipment worked. That is why this has become an argument over who deserves to own it.

We do not claim that an ingot carried years later proves what our furnace made. We have our own repair letters for the dates. The new sample helped somebody read an old material description. Let it remain a sample.

There are four signatures on the copy, and one space. The person who belongs in the space had left before the letter was passed around. We have asked for her last forwarding address. Until then, keep the space.

One contractor asked us to remove the account of purchases out of wages because it complicated the asset list. It complicated the wages first.

We are not asking Rivetline to decide a contract it never saw. We are asking that the name on the machine does not replace the names of the people who kept it working.

Attached note from Neri: I cannot settle the claim from these papers. I can retain the dates, the signed account and the distinction between an example and evidence. The blank space remains in the copy.

Last line, another hand: don't fill it with a manager's name just because his is easier to find.

spacertales-galley-account-file.name: GALLEY_ACCOUNT.TXT
spacertales-galley-account-file.text:
VERDEMORROW ARCHIVE: GALLEY PHOTOGRAPH
Crew account, held with the original caption

The jacket in the photograph belonged to the visiting dealer. It was cleaner than ours. Someone suggested it would look better in the picture. Later the picture became evidence of the contractor's provision programme.

I tended the crop. Sen cooked the meal. Alin fitted the rack and was still owed supper for the fitting. The programme did not include the nutrient charge I lent the dealer. He returned it after the photograph had travelled further than any of us.

The meal was good. I would like that sentence to survive whatever happens to the argument. We were tired and there was something green on a working ship. Not a miracle, not a farm, not a reason to stop buying supplies. Just something we had kept alive until it was ready.

There was stock set aside for another planting. Someone put it beside the meal ingredients. Sen moved it and wrote NOT SUPPER on the packet. I believe that is where the version of the story in our letter began. I don't claim to have invented the label.

I don't remember the tray weights, the room readings or how much water we had left when the photograph was taken. Please do not invent figures for a better caption. I remember who helped.

If you keep the contractor's caption, keep this with it. The jacket was real and so was the meal. One was borrowed. The other was work.

Archive note: the present product comparison was recorded separately. It establishes no historical yield or crop conditions. The new caption retains the names above. The meal owed to the installer remains in the copy of the first invoice.

spacertales-asterel-repair-file.name: TOMORROW_REPAIR.TXT
spacertales-asterel-repair-file.text:
ASTEREL SERVICE FILE: PLATE NUMBER RETAINED
Ship name struck through twice

To the next person on watch,

The office calls the board obsolete. That means the quotation for a new board has been filed. It does not mean the old one has stopped being our problem.

I am leaving the actual repair detail in the service record, where the next technician can check it. Do not use this covering letter as an operating instruction. I had the board in front of me. You may have a different fault.

When it came back into service the captain asked whether it would get us home. I said the ship would get us home if we kept the ship fit to do it. The board would help with its part. She found that answer irritating, so I wrote it down.

We called it Tomorrow because every replacement promise ended with that word. By the time the new quotation arrived, the ship had another name and the office could not connect it to the old record. Asterel still had the plate number. That is why the letter reached this file at all.

There is nothing brave about leaving someone else a fault you understand and they do not. Leave the record. Leave the date. If you borrowed a part, leave whose it was.

No one here needs the story to become a triumph over maintenance. It was maintenance. It worked because somebody did it.

Asterel archive note: the covering letter is reproduced as a crew account. It does not extend a warranty or establish the present condition of any module. The detailed repair record is not included in this public copy.

Name in the lower margin: Tomorrow. Written carefully, as if that were the part worth preserving.

spacertales-four-leaflets-file.name: FOUR_LEAFLETS.TXT
spacertales-four-leaflets-file.text:
ORRA PELL: QUOTATION RETURNED
Mixed shipboard plant, no order placed

Fennmark supplied a clear description of its equipment and stores. Tolvane supplied a clear description of the AX-2's job. Lixivar named its supported feed and products. Oxsmith described its hot route and the equipment needed around it. Four descriptions can all be accurate while the quotation joining them is incomplete.

The customer asked which vessel would receive each output, which line would connect it and where the heat would go. The proposed bill had a list of machines followed by installation as agreed. Nothing had been agreed.

One distributor offered a common finish. The customer had asked for a complete job, not common paint. I returned that offer with the original questions.

A service representative said I was asking each maker to guarantee the others' machines. I was asking the seller to identify what it was selling. Those are different requests.

The order has been paused. The owner can keep using the equipment already aboard, consider a smaller supported job or ask for a clearer proposal. No plant has been installed as a result of this correspondence. No joint service agreement exists.

I used to end files like this with sale lost. The customer says the sale was never complete enough to lose. I have left the final line blank.

Orra

Reply from the customer: leave the lists in the file. We may still need the right one for the right job. Put the empty space where the promised connection would have been.

spacertales-pump-accounts-file.name: PUMP_ACCOUNTS.TXT
spacertales-pump-accounts-file.text:
ALEMBRINE CUSTOMER STORY: TWO ACCOUNTS
The borrowed pump

First account: a bottle was sent to the ship from which the pump had been borrowed. The owner opened it, accepted an apology and agreed to stop asking for the pump during every conversation. That is described as a reconciliation. The pump was not returned.

Second account: the bottle reached the ship after it had changed owners. The new owner accepted it as a welcome gift and knew nothing about the pump. The old owner learned about the gift, asked why strangers had been sent an apology intended for him, and began asking for the pump in writing. That is described as the beginning of the quarrel.

Both accounts identify ordinary Alembrine stock. Neither identifies a special batch. Neither gives a reliable forwarding address for the pump.

The service department was asked whether its equipment produced the bottle. It could describe the supported process. It could not establish where a particular old bottle had been made from two contradictory letters.

The publicity department asked whether both accounts could be combined. The archive said they could be kept together, which is different.

A present-day bottle was compared with the product description and retained by its owner. It does not settle the old correspondence.

Unsent dealer copy: Alembrine, bringing people together.

Archive annotation: omit. The second account does not support this.

Final reply from the pump's owner: you have sent me two accounts of the bottle. I have asked about the pump.

No subsequent reply is retained.

spacertales-short-return-file.name: SHORT_RETURN.TXT
spacertales-short-return-file.text:
SHORT RETURN: FITTING AND WATCH LETTERS
Halewright service archive copy

Loading plan, first version: cargo occupies the proposed space around the bed. Crew can move it if care is needed.

Reply: tell me which person is moving it if the person on the bed is the one who normally moves it.

Loading plan, second version: approach kept clear. Supplies in the drawer. Cargo moved elsewhere before departure.

The surviving letters next concern a return to dock. They do not record enough clinical information to diagnose the patient, measure recovery or credit a particular treatment. Do not add a success rate to this file.

Watchkeeper's letter: the bed was supplied. The monitor was supplied. The watch was not supplied by either machine. People stayed, fetched what was needed and made sure there was a way to reach the person lying there.

I am glad the equipment was available. I am also glad somebody remembered it needed a room with air and reliable power, not only a place on an inventory. If you copy the invoice, copy the names in the next paragraph.

The names have been retained in the private correspondence. This public copy does not identify the patient. The former crew authorised the following final line: everyone we expected back reached dock.

Later note: the ship was sold. The bed and cart went to different buyers. Nobody could buy the watch with them. Keep the letters together, please.

Archive annotation: this is a crew account and a fitting history. The Vigil-2 observes; it does not treat. No medical outcome is certified by preserving the correspondence.

spacertales-two-drawings-file.name: TWO_DRAWINGS.TXT
spacertales-two-drawings-file.text:
SECOND-SHIFT LEDGER: TWO DRAWINGS
Covering correspondence only

The old drawing was supplied with the ship. It named every compartment the seller remembered to name. There was no galley where our galley now stood, and a doorway led through a place we had since made into somebody's bunk.

After the damage, the contractor's office sent back the old drawing as the repair authority. We asked whether the office wanted the missing wall put back or the last few years of our lives put somewhere else.

The crew drawing showed the ship after the last refit. It had rubbed-out lines, two notes saying check this and a stain the office called unauthorised. It also showed the parts we were actually trying to replace.

The old drawing was once accurate. The newer one was accurate where it had been checked. Neither became better evidence because the paper was cleaner.

We sent both. The office accepted a traced copy of the new one. Then it filed the old one beneath it because that was the original document. I expect somebody will reverse their order when they next decide to tidy the file.

Neri's note: these are letters about a historical dispute. No schematic is included, and nothing in this copy should be loaded as a repair plan for [ship].

The drawing you keep for work should say what you mean to keep aboard. The drawing you keep for memory can say what used to be there. A ship has room in its history for both.

A name appears beside the old bunk, then is crossed out. We have not removed it from the copy.

spacertales-loading-fee-file.name: LOADING_FEE.TXT
spacertales-loading-fee-file.text:
SLINGWRIGHT PUBLICITY: FEE DISPUTE
Signed worker's account

I agreed to be photographed beside a working RM-1. The first photograph showed the plant after we finished loading and cleared the space. The caption said the feeder cleared the machinery room.

The machine did what it was supplied to do with the feed it accepted. It did not walk around collecting the remainder stock. We loaded it. The clear room was also a record of that work.

Sales asked for a second photograph showing the loading, to correct the first caption. I asked for the loading time to be included in the new fee. They said the second photograph corrected the first agreement and therefore came under the first payment.

I said the first payment had covered a photograph, not a shift of carrying material and not a second photograph to make the first one accurate.

The archive wanted to know whether I was unhappy with the machine. I was unhappy with the account of the work. The machine was one part of that account.

The revised caption says a worker supplies accepted remainder stock to the feeder. The fee dispute remains a fee dispute. Accurate wording is useful, but I cannot pay my berth with it.

Slingwright annotation: retained under customer correspondence rather than image corrections. No claim is made about a customer's present feed, machinery operation or reaction-mass supply.

Last note in the worker's hand: you remembered the word supplied this time. Next time remember who supplied it.
